facts.value: £170,648,786 at 31 March 2026, up £2.2m — PWLB £130,399,760, interest-free borrowing £8,302,881, LOBOs £15,000,000, energy/Salix loans £5,414,652, 'Ex LOBO' £5,000,000, temporary borrowing £5,000,000 and accrued interest £1,531,493

source.title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 28 May 2026

facts.note: Section 8. All six half-yearly columns of the table foot exactly. Net borrowing £143.4m, down from £156.2m. In the year they took six long-term PWLB loans totalling £40m, one £5m temporary loan from another local authority and £5.2m of Salix, repaid £40m of short-term borrowing and made £8.45m of EIP payments.

facts.value: NOT STATED — Appendix B carries the prudential indicators and is not held

source.title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 28 May 2026

facts.note: There is no CFR, no prudential indicator value and no liability benchmark figure in what we have. THE BALANCE SHEET IDENTITY CANNOT BE CLOSED AND MUST NOT BE ASSERTED. §19 notes that the 'Proportion of financing costs to net revenue stream' indicator will need to be finalised once the year-end work on finance leases is complete.

facts.value: THREE LOBOs have call dates WITHIN THE NEXT TWELVE MONTHS, against £15,000,000 of LOBOs outstanding

source.title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 28 May 2026

facts.note: Section 10, verbatim: 'The other three LOBOs also have call dates within the next 12 months. Again, if the option is exercised and an increased rate proposed, a decision on how to proceed considering other financing options would be made in conjunction with our treasury advisors.' Newport has already exited LOBOs twice: the balance fell from £30,000,000 at September 2023 to £15,000,000 at March 2024, and a separate £5,000,000 sits on a line labelled 'Ex LOBO'. Across the sector we now hold TWELVE LOBO calls across nine councils and every one was refused and the loan repaid or refinanced.

facts.value: £40m of PWLB taken in the first half of the year when rates 'dipped', producing larger than normal investment balances

source.title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 28 May 2026

facts.note: Sections 6 and 12 and the CFO's comment. Investments rose £13.8m to £27.4m as a result. The CFO records that 'holding costs in undertaking this borrowing in advance of need were small' and that 'Given the recent rise in bond yields... this strategy has served the Council well but it will inevitably need to borrow externally again as the current year progresses.'

facts.value: £5.2m of Salix energy loans taken in the year, which §6 says 'offer a significantly better rate of interest than loans which the Council can get from the PWLB'

source.title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 28 May 2026

facts.note: The balance went from £230,974 to £5,414,652 — a movement of £5,183,678, exactly the stated £5.2m. The only place in the sector where we have seen a council state plainly that another lender beat the PWLB on price.

facts.value: £27.4m at 31 March 2026, up £13.8m, including three covered bonds held to maintain MiFID II professional client status

source.title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 28 May 2026

facts.note: Sections 12 and 13. The bonds are Santander £3.5m, Lloyds £4m and Cie de Financement Foncier £2.5m, bought in February 2023 to meet the £10m minimum balance criterion. The risk table also records that the Council 'withdrew its investment from one local authority recently' — the only credit-driven withdrawal from the inter-authority market we have seen disclosed anywhere.

facts.value: £1.5m of one-off funding agreed at Cabinet in February 2026 as a VOLUNTARY minimum revenue payment, to reduce capital financing pressures over the five-year rolling programme

source.title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 28 May 2026

facts.note: Section 29. A voluntary MRP is a deliberate acceleration of debt repayment and is rare in the reports we read.

facts.value: a net DISCOUNT of about £5.9m — balance £116,064,279, indicative settlement £110,124,144

source.title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 28 May 2026

facts.note: OUR figure, not theirs. DMO premature repayment curve, notice 314/26 PM, 14 August 2026. 29 of 31 priced. 15 loans below par (£59,681,054 principal, £8,307,612 of discount); 14 above (£56,383,225, £2,367,478 of premium) — one of the most evenly balanced books in the library, with almost half the principal on each side of par. INDICATIVE ONLY — only the DMO can quote.

source.title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 28 May 2026

summary.text:
Newport's outturn report has the most actionable single item of the batch and no way to act on it: paragraph 10 records that THREE of its LOBOs have call dates within the next twelve months, against £15,000,000 outstanding — and the report publishes no officer name at all, only titles.

That matters because of what we now hold. Twelve LOBO calls across nine councils since the spring — Harrow's £20.8m, Staffordshire's £15m and ten others — and every single one was refused and the loan repaid or refinanced. Not one borrower has accepted a higher rate. Newport has already been through it twice on its own book: LOBOs fell from £30,000,000 at September 2023 to £15,000,000 at March 2024, and a separate £5,000,000 sits on an 'Ex LOBO' line.

The arithmetic is exceptionally clean. The §8 table carries six half-yearly positions across seven categories and every one of the six columns foots exactly. The stated £2.2m increase in borrowing decomposes across all seven rows to £2,210,149, with the accrued interest movement (£492,590 against a stated '£493k') and the Salix movement (£5,183,678 against '£5.2m') both exact. Our own file matches the PWLB row to the pound at £130,399,760.

Two other things of record. Paragraph 6 says the Salix energy loans 'offer a significantly better rate of interest than loans which the Council can get from the PWLB' — the only place in the sector we have seen that stated plainly — and the balance went from £230,974 to £5,414,652. And the risk table records that the Council 'withdrew its investment from one local authority recently', the only credit-driven withdrawal from the inter-authority market disclosed anywhere in our reading. No CFR appears (Appendix B not held), so nothing is asserted about the balance sheet.

officer.subject: Three LOBO calls ahead — here's what happened to the last twelve
officer.meeting: Governance and Audit Committee — report onward to Cabinet and Council; mid-year due winter 2026

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the outturn report that went to Governance and Audit on 28 May. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, and yours is one of the cleanest we have run. Our file holds 31 PWLB loans for Newport totalling exactly £130,399,760 — the same figure, to the pound, as the March 2025-26 row of your paragraph 8 table. That table carries six half-yearly positions across seven categories and every one of the six columns foots exactly, which is rarer than it should be. Better than that, your stated £2.2m increase in borrowing decomposes across all seven rows to £2,210,149, with the accrued interest movement coming out at £492,590 against your "£493k" and the Salix movement at £5,183,678 against your "£5.2m". We could rebuild the whole year from the table.

We wrote because of paragraph 10.

Three of your LOBOs have call dates within the next twelve months, and you say that if a rate increase is proposed the decision will be taken with your treasury advisers. We have been tracking LOBO calls across the sector since the spring, and what we have is probably the most useful thing we can offer you before those dates arrive.

Twelve calls, across nine councils. Every single one refused, and the loan repaid or refinanced. Not one authority in our file has accepted the new rate. The two largest were Harrow's £20.8m — their last remaining LOBO, called, declined and repaid, funded with £65m of new PWLB — and Staffordshire's £15m, called, declined and repaid early, with £18m of LOBOs still outstanding there. Dexia is the counterparty in six of the LOBO books we hold.

You have of course already been through this twice on your own book, which the table shows: LOBOs fell from £30,000,000 at September 2023 to £15,000,000 at March 2024, and a separate £5,000,000 has sat on the "Ex LOBO" line throughout. So none of this is new to Newport. What is new is the sector-wide count, because no single council can see it — you see your own calls, not whether anyone anywhere has taken the rate. As of this month, nobody has.

We are not suggesting what to do when a call comes; that is a conversation with Arlingclose and it depends on the rate proposed and what your alternatives cost on the day. The one figure worth having alongside it is what the alternatives cost. On this afternoon's notice, 314/26, certainty rates are 4.95% at one year, 5.34% at five, 5.83% at ten and 6.38% at twenty. Your existing PWLB book runs at a weighted 4.2541%.

Two smaller things, both of which we noted because they are unusual rather than because anything follows.

Your paragraph 6 says the Salix energy loans "offer a significantly better rate of interest than loans which the Council can get from the PWLB". That is the only place in everything we have read this year where a council states plainly that another lender beat the PWLB on price, and the balance moved from £230,974 to £5,414,652 in twelve months on the strength of it. If those schemes keep clearing, it is a funding line most authorities are not using at that scale.

And your risk table records that the Council "withdrew its investment from one local authority recently". That is the only credit-driven withdrawal from the inter-authority market we have seen disclosed anywhere. It is worth knowing that the market you stepped back from has been pricing very widely: over this year end it ran from about 4.15% to 8.50% depending on who needed money and when, with Cornwall paying 8.50% for four days and Gloucestershire borrowing £55m at 4.15% to 4.70%. Meanwhile the volume in it grew sharply — Staffordshire's lending book went from £30m to £152m across twenty-five councils, and Liverpool raised £118m of two-to-four-year money from seventeen. Wide spreads and rising volumes at the same time is the pattern worth watching, and it is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

Finally, for completeness on the debt side: on the DMO's repayment curve today your book sits almost exactly balanced — 15 loans below par carrying about £8.3m of discount and 14 above carrying £2.4m of premium, so roughly £5.9m net discount. That is one of the most evenly split books we have priced, and it is a consequence of yours being 17 EIP loans out of 31. We don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Newport. Alternatives to PWLB covers LOBOs and the sector's call record ahead of your three dates. Interest rate risk goes to paragraph 28. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets goes to the withdrawal in your risk table. PWLB repayment structures covers the EIP weighting. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
